survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: PIRLS 2006 is an international large-scale assessment with sampling designed to support cross-national comparability, including careful selection of representative schools and students and extensive quality-control checks prior to analysis. The report describes that countries met rigorous sampling standards and that participation-rate guidelines were assessed (with notes where replacement schools were included). The document does not specify the exact student weight variable names (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used in the published tables. For analysts using PIRLS microdata, the appropriate complex survey weights and replicate design information should be applied to obtain correct standard errors under the study’s multistage sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is an official PIRLS international report that primarily reports scaled achievement results, benchmark attainment percentages, and descriptive relationships between contextual indices and reading achievement. The excerpted text does not document a specific PV-based analytic pipeline (e.g., Rubin’s rules, PV averaging) or a missing-data handling procedure for an empirical predictive model. Missingness is discussed descriptively for questionnaire coverage (e.g., parent questionnaire missingness thresholds), but no explicit imputation/deletion rule for an achievement PV analysis is provided in the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: PIRLS 2006 targets students in the fourth year of formal schooling (typically fourth grade), with a policy minimum average age of 9.5 years for paper-and-pencil testing. Most countries assessed fourth-grade students; Iceland and Norway also assessed smaller samples in fifth grade, and additional fifth-grade testing occurred in England, New Zealand, Scotland, Trinidad and Tobago, and in Luxembourg and South Africa due to language-of-instruction constraints. Sampling was conducted with representative school and student samples per country, with extensive translation verification and consistency/comparability checks across countries prior to analysis. The report also notes that some questionnaire-based exhibits use notations when parent questionnaire data coverage is below certain thresholds (r/s/x), but it does not specify a single analytic deletion/imputation rule for achievement outcomes in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: PIRLS 2006 is an international large-scale assessment of reading comprehension in primary schools, administered to students in the fourth year of formal schooling (typically fourth grade) across 40 countries plus additional participating education systems/provinces (45 participants total). The assessment measures reading for two purposes—literary experience and acquiring/using information—across four comprehension processes (retrieving explicitly stated information, making straightforward inferences, interpreting/integrating ideas, and examining/evaluating content). Achievement is reported on a PIRLS reading scale (mean 500, SD 100) and anchored to four international benchmarks (Low 400, Intermediate 475, High 550, Advanced 625), with benchmark attainment reported as cumulative percentages. The report also provides trend comparisons with PIRLS 2001 for a subset of participants and describes how contextual indices (e.g., early home literacy activities, home educational resources, parental attitudes) relate to reading achievement. In the provided text, no predictive ML modeling is conducted; results are descriptive and benchmark-based, so causal claims cannot be inferred.
